speechtext:
I wish to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, for making this debate possible here tonight and for the opportunity to put forward thoughts on all sides of the House and to deal with what seems to most of us to be the major facets of this issue. To me, the facets are the question of prevention, the question of international standards and regulations, the issue of imposing moratoria, and finally, the most diffi-
April 4, 1989

cult issue of long-term energy policy and our dependence on oil.
Before I go into that, I would like to draw to your attention a curious pattern which develops whenever the Conservative Government finds itself in trouble in matters related to the environment. It conveniently hides behind three claims. The first one, and we have heard it many times before in other debates, and it is the most ludicrous of them all, is that everything that is positive in the environment achieved by Governments began in 1985.
Second, when the heat gets a bit too high it trots out this new element of the Prime Ministers of Canada being hailed abroad and receiving awards. That helps enormously.
Third, when that fails to make an impression on this side of the Elouse, it comes up with this beautiful convincing item saying that Canadians do not like partisanship in the environment. We must all say the same thing. We must unite. We must be supportive of the shortcomings and the failures of this Government. Tonight, two hours ago, the present Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) followed the examples of his two predecessors and did exactly the same thing. What a sham!
The question is what are the steps, the substantial steps, that the Government has taken to ensure that our own practices and regulations at home and those of our neighbors are taken into account and enforced so as to ensure prevention. The question here is a very crucial one because prevention is much more important than reaction. Even the most speedy and quick reaction which the Minister of the Environment invoked in his intervention is not as good as prevention. He will agree with that.
We must find ways of increasing this prevention. How this Government can increase prevention when it has over the years lost its main muscle financially to maintain in the Department of the Environment 330 people which it has lost over the last four years, and with a budget that has not been able to keep up with inflation, is hard to understand. In other words, one can prevent if one has the budget available to carry out that prevention. If one is losing ground to other Departments and to inflation, then the instruments available to Ministers disappear as well. That is what struck me as the weakest measure, the
weakest part of the ministerial interventions here tonight.
The problem with the Conservatives is that they are still part of the problem. They are strong on rhetoric but they are weak on substance. When they cannot maintain the strength in their own Department of the Environment, and in Departments that are allied to it, in preventive measures in our marine environment, then one can only react. The necessary preventive measures cannot be taken to be ahead in this game.
There were some interventions tonight also on the matter of international standards for pilots and for the prosecution of companies. It is ridiculous to see in the situation of Exxon that the person who has to pay is the captain and not the company. It is ridiculous to see in the case of Exxon a situation whereby highly qualified, trained pilots are not in charge of the supertanker. Evidently there is something in this whole industry that must be established that is missing.
We must learn from the aviation industry, borrow from the standards that have been established there, and move very quickly internationally to ensure that the marine pilots are of the same competence as the pilots in the air and that those who are guilty of offences, the companies that are guilty of offences, are prosecuted and not the individual.
The lesson is that prevention requires budgets. The Conservatives are part of the problem. With respect to the same steps that have been taken in Washington to which the Minister alluded very vaguely tonight, it is not known what they are leading us to.
What has been done in Washington since this spill on the West Coast is something that the public should know. That should also be debated here so that we can intelligently participate in the building of these new approaches which are so badly needed.
We must also call on the Government, as have others, to hold a public inquiry into Canada's ability to deal quickly with major spills in our water. That is an aspect that also should be made public in the interests of the public and in the interests of all those fine environmental principles which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) invokes when he goes abroad but which he seems to forget when he comes back to Ottawa.
It seems to us also that we must put on hold future offshore exploration projects until the results of such an inquiry are known. It would be a wise course of action.

April 4, 1989
It would also be desirable to impose a moratorium, possibly in perpetuity, on offshore oil exploration in the Hackett Strait and in the Dixon Entrance for very well known reasons that could be defined if time were available.
It would be desirable to impose a moratorium, possibly in perpetuity, on tanker traffic in Lancaster Sound and in the Northwest Passage. This could happen to us as well one day. We do not want one day to have our fragile Arctic ecology damaged by the movement of tankers through the Northwest Passage and through Lancaster Sound. We have the opportunity now in the light of enormous public pressure and intense public opinion to move on this desirable front.
Finally, as others have before me, we are brought to ask ourselves whether the time has not arrived for us to discuss our long-term energy policy and the fact that we can and must find ways of using more efficiently our oil resources globally, in North America to begin with, and also find ways of developing alternative sources of energy so that we will not depend on oil that has to be shipped from the northern regions to the southern markets.
I see that my time has come to an end. I would like to conclude by saying this. As the proverb states, an ounce of prevention is much more effective than a pound of reaction. The Minister of the Environment, I am sure, would want to have the budgets at his disposal to be preventive out there on the West Coast of Canada as it is desirable for him and his Government to be. We are looking forward to seeing what the Budget will contain to provide this Minister the tools that he needs. We can assure him that if he gets the tools he needs we will support him and applaud him. If he does not get the tools he needs then we will know that on the Conservative side of this House what is being said on the environment is rhetoric, not supported and followed up by substance.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Coast Guard is lead agency for all marine source spills. As soon as the first site of the oil spill was discovered in the Nestucca incident, the Coast Guard mounted a full operational response. This response included all of the relevant federal and provincial organizations. Altogether over 350 people worked at the peak of the clean-up. This comprised the largest team of environmental and scientific operational personnel ever assembled on the West Coast to address the clean-up operations and the environmental impact assessment. The primary clean-up was undertaken by the ship owner's contractors under supervision of the Canadian Coast Guard.
Under both Canadian and American law, the polluter is responsible for all costs, expenses, and direct damages associated with the marine oil spill. Supporting the response was a team comprised of federal and provincial agencies such as the Department of the Environment and Fisheries and Oceans. The military assisted by providing helicopters and aircraft support.
At the peak of the clean-up operations responding agencies in the contract deployed up to 10 vessels, 13 helicopters and surveillance aircraft, command posts and various other resources. To date over 370 tonnes of oil and oil-related debris have been recovered, most of which is stored at the interim site at Cassidy. Operations were completed on March 19, and the monitoring phase commenced on March 20.
In response to marine pollution accidents, the Canadian Coast Guard has a multilevel contingency plan in place which deals with incidents on a local, regional and international level. In conjunction with the supporting Departments, the Coast Guard conducts exercises to evaluate these plans and to provide training for the multi-disciplined teams, and in the Nestucca incident the joint marine pollution contingency plan was invoked. The Canadian Coast Guard also maintains depots of pollution counter-measures equipment at 50 locations across Canada. This inventory valued at $35 million is available for deployment to any location.
Mr. Speaker, as permanent environment damage is a great concern, a multi-disciplined team of federal-provincial experts was involved throughout the Nestucca response in assessing the spill impact. The scale of this impact assessment exceeded any other previously mounted, and will provide valuable information needed to assess long-term effects.
Mr. Speaker, it is the polluter's responsibility to settle any claims arising out of a spill directly with the claimants. To assist with the processing of claims, the Canadian Coast Guard established a claims assistance office to provide help and advance to potential claimants. The process for documenting claims is based on a system developed following the Kurdistan incident in 1979. Our lawyers are also actively studying every angle of Canadian and American law, to pursue Canadian claims for assistance. In addition the Government is attempting to assist in this process by establishing an appropriate procedure with the polluter for the processing of claims.
Mr. Speaker, the principle that the polluter is responsible for the damage caused by this spill also applies to economic losses. Moreover, as a last result, the Marine Pollution Claims Fund may also be available for economic loss suffered by fishermen.
In conclusion, following every incident a review of the response and operation is undertaken. Incidents such as the Nestucca are unfortunate and we all recognize the need to work hard to prevent reoccurences. In assessing the response and identifying areas for improvement, we are provided with the opportunity to improve our response.
Mr. Speaker, our Government cares, and in times of disaster we will respond to the best of our ability.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the only new Member of Parliament in Parliament here, it is my pleasure to speak on behalf of the Inuit of Nunatsiaq and as a representative of the northern people. I am pleased to speak tonight, although it pains me that it had to come to this point before we were able to speak on this issue. This is a disaster of very large consequences and it is part of our land because Inuit occupy a circumpolar world all across from Alaska to Greenland to Canada and to the Soviet Union. So we consider the North as part of our land, and we don't define any international boundaries between the people of the various international regions.

April 4, 1989
The Valdez spill disaster must cause us all to think about the environment and the costs of such accidents.
As a northerner whose people depend to a large extent on the land, the ocean and its resources, the possibility of a spill like this in the Canadian Arctic is extremely disturbing. The North cannot afford such a disaster.
The North wants and needs development but not at any cost. The National Energy Board will soon begin hearings on applications by Shell, Esso, and Gulf for 20-year licences to export natural gas from the Mackenzie Delta to the United States. A pipeline will be necessary to transport that gas if the applications are approved.
Although times have changed since the Berger Inquiry, and land claims are close to being achieved for the Dene and Metis of the western Arctic and the Inuit of central and eastern Arctic, and the Innuvialuit claim was settled in 1984, there is still the concern that development will proceed. I reiterate that we are not against development to the extent that we can be sure it will be safe for all the people of the Northwest Territories and Alaska.
At the same time, the President of the United States has been considering development or exploration in an area known as 10.0.2 at the Alaska-Yukon border. This land covers the grounds of the Porcupine Caribou herd. President Bush has indicated that the Exxon disaster does not affect whether the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge should be developed because that disaster was likely a result of human error. Most developmental disasters are a result of human error, and I beg to differ with President Bush on this issue.
The full Congress has yet to make a decision on this development. However, there has been much discussion on the issue and it is likely that exploration on this development will begin. If passed, the legislature would be giving its stamp of approval to the opening of the coastal plain of the refuge to environmentally responsible oil and gas exploration, development and protection. As we all aware, however, no development is safe from
disaster, whether it is through human error or other means.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will visit President Bush in the near future. His trip will include environmental discussions, including initiatives for the Arctic. The Prime Minister will also receive an environmental award from the International Chamber of Commerce on May 4. I question the merit of this award, based on the slowness of the Government's response to the Exxon Valdez disaster. We have been told by various Ministers that the effect of that disaster is not approaching Canadian waters. The animals in that area, whether it is the seals, whales, salmon or any other wildlife, know no boundaries.
While the Government of the Northwest Territories has approved in principle the building of the pipeline because of the need for economic development in the North, it is qualified by the fact that environmental concerns must be safeguarded.
As the only Inuit Member of Parliament and representative of the true North, which is supposedly strong and free, I have very grave concerns about the whole issue unless there are stringent regulations in effect.
Our people are taught by our elders early in life that above all we must honour the lands, the water, and all that is within them.
The straightforward lesson is communicating to one and all, for our people know that we have survived for thousands of years in all types of conditions because we valued, respected, and honoured all that was around us. We came to understand that rather than forcing the environment to conform to our needs, we developed behaviour that adapts to our environment. How incredibly it is sad that I stand here tonight, believing as strongly as I do in the wisdom of the Inuit elders, and see a situation in which our man-made systems and processes have dealt such a painful life threatening blow to this fragile and unique part of the world. I know that native people in Alaska must share a similar philosophy. They surely must be shaking their heads as they watch the events that are unfolding in their land.
They have lived through various occupations in their land and have seen a steady stream of visitors come to dabble with technology that they swore was failure-proof in an environment in which man can never and should never attempt to rule.
We hear stories of carelessness, recklessness, over confidence, alcoholism, debauchery and gross ignorance
April 4, 1989

on the part of tanker crews and carpet-baggers at Valdez. How must native people feel, along with non-native Alaskans who live off the land and water, being forced into a situation where all the boastful experts were suddenly rendered powerless and ineffectual, drowning along with wildlife in their own technology?
If we are going to develop the North, whether it is in Alaska, Canada or anywhere else in our circumpolar world, we must take finto consideration the people who have lived there for thousands of years without any man-made disasters. It is because they know how to live off the land. People must listen to them rather than making decisions in the boardrooms of America or southern Canada. If they are not heard, I predict more disasters of this type as a result of the carelessness of the developers.

On November 21 the people of Victoria and Vancouver Island voted for strong, effective, and progressive voices in Parliament. They voiced their deep concern especially with the issues of the environment. We have in today's emergency debate had a clear demonstration that indeed Vancouver Island and Victoria have finally found their full voice in this House of Commons.
It is really a profound shame that this debate is taking place. If anything good comes of it, it may be that, finally, this Government will get the message that the West Coast exists, that we have real problems and that we will insist that these concerns are addressed in Parliament.
The Speech from the Throne contained many words about the environment and many noble intentions of the Government. A closer reading, however, indicates that the central Canadian perspective of the Government is fully heard in the speech. For example, it contains no reference whatever to the Alaska oil spill, the worst oil spill in the history of North America. It contains no reference whatever to the West coast oil spill that occurred in December and January.
The oil spill we are debating tonight is in fact the twelfth worst oil spill in the history of this planet. I have here a list of the other oil spills. Many of them are common knowledge including the Torrey Canyon, Amoco Cadiz and others.
Despite the fact that this is the worst oil spill in North American history, there was not one word in the Speech from the Throne about it. There was not one word in it about West Coast oil spills. There was talk of cleaning up the problems in the St. Lawrence River. There was talk about cleaning up the problems of acid rain in the Great Lakes and the problems of the Arctic, but there was not one word about the environmental concerns of the sensitive ecological system on the West Coast.
There was not one word in the Speech from the Throne about another subject, forestry, the Carmanah Creek and the Carmanah Valley, the crisis in our forest industry, the overcutting, the problem of job losses in Fletcher Challenge and elsewhere. However, because of the initiative of the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) and your response, Mr. Speaker, we are having this important debate.
It is worth while to notice that Ministers of the Government have participated in the debate, a healthy sign that they are finally at least forced to explain themselves on the floor of the House of Commons.
I want to put a series of specific proposals to the House. First, I propose that there should be a formal public inquiry into oil spills on the West Coast. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) said that as a result of the oil spills this was the occasion to examine the response of the Government. He said, "of course it will be done." What we say to the Minister is, do not make it an internal departmental inquiry. Instead, make it an open, public inquiry which environmental groups and experts have an opportunity to attend. Give them an opportunity to examine and cross-examine witnesses. Provide them with some resources so that their views can be heard on this very important issue. This is one way to begin to restore some confidence in the whole system of government and in its capacity to respond to the perceived dangers on the West Coast.
Second, we call for an immediate statement as to which Department of Government is responsible for dealing with oil spills. We hear from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard). He has not found it possible, I gather, to attend all parts of this debate. I hope he is listening. The Minister of the Environment seems to take a lead. We hear from the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) and from three Ministers of State from British Columbia. It is not clear who is in charge of

April 4, 1989
this problem nor was it clear who was in charge when the west coast spill occurred in December and January. Reports from the front indicated all kinds of chaos, confusion, and disarray. In fact, there was said to be a bureaucratic war going on as to who was actually in charge. The time has come to make it very clear publicly who is accountable for responding to oil spills.
Third, we ask for thorough consultation with environmental and municipal people on Vancouver Island.
Fourth, we ask that there should be compensation for those in the tourist industry and in the fishing industry who have suffered damage from oil spills. It should not be the responsibility of individual Canadians to pursue costly international litigation. The Government should provide immediate compensation and then undertake the litigation itself.
Fifth, we ask for a moratorium on offshore drilling. Sixth, we look to the Government to give some genuine attention to research and development in this area. There has been in my own constituency of Victoria the development of OSCAR. OSCAR is a process for responding to oil spills. It uses quite a different technology from the skimming process that has been used. It is a development which is being pressed by people with long experience in the oil industry and in the marine industry. It is Canadian technology. It is endorsed by private users. We see this as an opportunity to develop Canadian technology, to use Canadian brains and responses to deal with these very difficult environmental disasters, and we would ask the Minister to give this very thorough and independent consideration.
Seventh, we ask that there be imposed standards and controls on all tankers and barges using our territorial waters. Part of the problem we face in Victoria, for example, is that four to six tankers are going by the Straits of Juan de Fuca within just a few miles of Victoria, and these are aging tankers. They are a moving ecological disaster waiting to happen. It will happen, as the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca (Mr. Barrett) said, unless this Government moves promptly to impose standards and controls.
Finally, we ask the Government to review the recommendations of the tri-level task force which reported in January.
The Valdez and West Coast oil spills are a warning to the people of Canada, indeed to the people of the world, of what we are doing to our environment. The issue here
is not just oil spills. The issue is what we are doing ecologically to this planet.
Once again, people are ahead of their Governments. They are demanding, and we endorse and put forward that demand in the House of Commons, that we treat the challenge to our environment as the fundamental issue of our time. Time is short. We must move to develop alternative energy sources, and a revolution in our way of approaching transportation and fuel. We have to look at new ways of conservation. We must develop a completely new way of addressing the problems that we face.
This has been an important debate. I urge the Government to endorse the ideas put forward.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last 90 days in my riding, I spent hours and hours talking to many of my constituents, and the number one issue on their agenda was the environment. There is a passionate view, not just in my riding but I believe in all ridings across Canada, that we have a very special opportunity here to set an international standard, an international model, in terms of following recommendations from the Brundtland Commission.
When I came back here on Monday and I listened to the Speech from the Throne, I was really excited. I heard words like, "Canadians possess a unique sense of their relationship to the land whose rich, vast diversity has shaped their values and experience and throughout the regions and across all linguistic and ethnic communities there is a shared concern that we protect our environment for generations of future Canadians," and on it went in the Speech from the Throne. "The national round table on the environment and other initiatives are part of a new environmental agenda which will also include commitments to certain things," and on and on it went. I left the Senate Chamber feeling very excited.
As the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) noted earlier tonight, probably never in the history of a Speech from the Throne have we heard so much in terms of a national Government's commitment to the environment.
We love our country and we all have a vision of it. I believe on this issue the challenge is to take this vision and this feeling we have all talked about and turn it into reality. Earlier tonight the Minister spoke about a non-partisan approach to the environment. I think that is a great way to go in this issue. Again, that statement must become reality. How does that non-partisan approach work? I just do not understand the logic. If we
April 4, 1989

are taking a non-partisan approach to the issue, then why would we not have this formal public inquiry? What is wrong with having a formal public inquiry? It does not make sense to me when we follow the logic of us all working together.
Here we are less than 40 hours after the Speech from the Throne and I am concerned that we are going to be following into the trap of the "mad" treatment, the maximum administrative delay. I say to the Minister he cannot fall into this trap on this issue. This is an issue where we must move with all of the political will of all of the Parties in this House. I am not really sure that we have done our best on this. I am not really sure nor am I convinced that the words of non-partisanship are really as genuine as they sound. I think this issue is a terrific example and an opportunity for us to begin turning those words into action. Even here tonight the Minister can pre-empt me and say I have no problem with a formal public inquiry.
This incident is in the United States but this issue is a global environmental issue. This Minister of the Environment has an opportunity to set a world-class example. There is no one in this House, there is no one in this country who will not back him on this issue as long as we are all working together and as long as we are achieving the common future. I believe that if we are going to get this session on the right foot, we should begin by focusing on the words "let's turn vision into reality". Here is an example where we can show not only Canadians whom we are encouraging to get involved in this issue but we can set an example for our American friends, for our friends all around the world that we are serious, that we will collaborate with them because even collaborating on this issue will be helpful to us, God forbid, should it ever happen in Canada.
Through you, Mr. Speaker, I urge the Minister to make sure that the words in the Speech from the Throne are not words that are diversionary, they are not words that are just rhetoric but words of substance and words of action.
As my colleague from Davenport said earlier this evening, if the Minister acts on these issues in a straightforward manner without an administrative delay approach I know he will have the support of my colleagues.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 52   ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS VALDEZ OIL SPILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a particular interest in the urgent debate so appropriately brought forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton). In this debate I am talking not
only about a community far away, Valdez, Alaska, but my neighbour Alaska. Many of us in the Yukon, in my riding, often visit Alaska. I have visited Valdez on numerous occasions. It is a beautiful community. To see the effects of what has happened with this oil spill is very close to me and close to people in my riding, to all northerners as some of my colleagues from other northern areas have explained, and also to my colleagues from British Columbia who have so recently at first-hand felt the effects of a serious oil spill.
The questions of oil and gas development and its ramifications, good and bad, on the northern economy and the environment are issues that are extremely close to home. It is impossible to live in the North and not be keenly aware of the fragility of the environment. For those of us who have participated in the past in pipeline hearings on the Beaufort Sea, all of the questions that are now coalescing around the Valdez oil spill and its ramifications not just for the United States but also for Canada really bring back memories of those discussions, and in many cases arguments about the feasibility of tanker travel in the North. There were many presentations made about the dangers of this, about the difficulties with shifting sea ice, with icebergs, and exactly the kinds of concerns that, alas, have been exemplified by the Valdez oil spill.
Once again in the North we will be into hearings on gas exports in the coming weeks and again the same issues of weighing the environment, the natural resource, the benefit, the revenue and the expenditure will become before the Canadian public.
Two of my colleagues have mentioned the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, a transboundary park in northern Yukon and Alaska. That happens to be the calving grounds of the Porcupine Caribou herd. That region was set aside because it is the calving grounds. The Porcupine Caribou herd represents not just 150,000 animals but a national and international treasure and a non-renewable resource. However, we see that the American Government is beginning to reconsider its position and is beginning to look at possible drilling on these lands. The Americans are weighing this drilling against the non-renewable international heritage-what are best estimates of the amount of oil recoverable from the lands as being an oil supply of two years for the United States. This is two years of oil versus an irreplaceable international treasure which also happens to be part of a very viable economic system for at least 12 or 15 aboriginal communities.

April 4, 1989
Those are the kinds of questions that the spill in Valdez again brings forward to our society and asks us to question what we value, and what kind of a system we have created and what some of the ramifications of that system are.
During many of the environmental hearings in which I have participated in the North the question has always come up about the possibility and risks of any kind of development. Some of those will be deemed to be acceptable. That is quite understandable, Mr. Speaker. Economic development, the use of natural resources for all Canadians and northerners, is an important consideration. But the risks are often calculated on a very interesting basis. They are calculated on the risk to the investor, often the oil and gas developer. Rarely are the risks identified. In many ways we have not been able to identify in a realistic and calculable way the risks of exactly the kind of oil spill that has taken place in Valdez.
Earlier someone referred to the Amoco Cadiz case in France off the French coast in 1978. That tanker spilled 200,000 tonnes of crude oil. What were the costs? The French Government in that particular case had already spent $36.7 million on clean-up but could not even estimate the long-term effects on fishing and tourism. We are in exactly the same position, Mr. Speaker.
My colleagues have spoken about the possible effects of this spill as it moves towards the West Coast on the Tatsenshini and Alsek Rivers. Those two rivers supply subsistence fishing for many residents in the area, a commercial fishing industry, tourism, and a very vital environmental wilderness area that is part of the ecosphere and the fundamental environmental basis of the air we breathe and the waters that we drink.
We expect our Governments to act to protect us in these cases. I would like to support two things raised by my colleagues. First of all is most certainly the call for a public inquiry. Any Government, any Parliament, any group of politicians, and indeed citizens who believe what has become almost a cliche, sustainable development, and we should also be talking taking about sustainable environment, must have the opportunity for full and open inquiry when such an event as this happens.
We know that there is no quick fix solution. We know the Valdez oil spill has pointed out to us that the technology does not exist to do the clean-up required. In fact, taxpayers who often pay to encourage that development end up paying a second time to do the clean-up that might occur as a result of accidents such as that at Valdez. Clearly, the taxpayer has a vested interest in
such a public inquiry, not only for now but for the future and the long-term consequences for our children and grandchildren.
The previous speaker referred to having to examine the life-style that we have created and become dependent upon. When there was that little blip about the oil scare, Governments were encouraging alternate energy development. The programs of Energy, Mines and Resources in that regard have been cut back to nothing. The programs through Environment Canada to encourage conservation and to look at alternate energy resources in a long-term energy policy have been cut back to virtually nothing.
Canadian taxpayers have a right to know whether the Government is only talking about rhetoric when it comes to the environment. Both members of the Elouse and the Canadian public will therefore be looking very closely to the Budget to see if the Government is prepared to take into account seriously the long-term needs concerning the environment of this country, and indeed that of the international issues.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have to admit some puzzlement at the obviously defensive attitude that appears to have been taken by a number of the speakers and Ministers opposite, in particular the Member for Vancouver Centre (Ms. Campbell).
This debate tonight is not about the Vancouver Island oil spill. It is not about who or what caused the Valdez oil spill, or is it for the wringing of hands with respect to the tragic aftermath of these spills.
This debate is an alarm bell for all Canadians. It is an alarm bell that signals that Canadians do not have confidence in the ability of the Government to prevent an oil spill of significant size such as occurred recently, nor the confidence that the Government has the ability to clean and limit an oil spill such as occurred recently. It is a warning bell not only of that perception, but also that we are not prepared.
We have heard tonight from the Ministers responsible that we have equipment, we have manpower, and we have know-how dispersed across the country, dispersed strategically waiting for the next emergency to occur. That is exactly what we would have heard from Exxon two weeks ago. It would have said exactly the same thing. What did that get for our American neighbours at Valdez? It got them nothing.
We have heard the same rhetoric here today as the Ministers have read from their Ministry briefings listing the many tools, devices, know-how, and skills at our disposal to deal with these things. We know, and Cana-
April 4, 1989

dians know, that we have not done enough. The proof is in every successive oilspill. They just keep on coming. Every spill and every sea-life kill proves that we still have not yet done enough. That is why we have a crisis in confidence, and that is why we have the debate tonight.
We also know that we do have ways and means to improve. We need vastly improved standards of navigational safety, and we need vastly improved standards in international shipping and international agreements governing the transport of oil.
Why have the Ministers here today, the Ministers who purport to represent all Canadians in matters such as this, Transport, Environment, and Fisheries and Oceans not discussed the improvements that we can and must make? Why has there been no mention of these? It is because they are not there, and that is why there is a crisis in confidence.
We have heard the ministerial rhetoric, and we have heard the travelogues about the beautiful B.C. coast, but that does not get us improvement. We have Armed Forces that have said to us time and time again in this changing world where the Armed Forces will do more than simply shoot bullets, to tell them what to do, give them the tools and they will do the job. Still I see nothing on this.
We have areas where international agreement governing the transport of oil and other commodities could improve the safety conditions, because it is not only rules that prevent these spills, but will assist in preventing these types of spills.
It is my hope that the Ministers opposite will not continue to be blinded by their own rhetoric and the rhetoric of their Ministries that they have done enough and we are ready. I will not permit the Ministers or the Government, and my Party will not permit them to be trapped by the rhetoric of their Ministries. If anything is to be gained from our debate here tonight it will be a recognition by Canadians that the Government of today realizes its own weaknesses in this regard, both real and perceived, and believe me they are perceived, and that the Government will take concrete steps to resolve those weaknesses and thus help to prevent absolutely another Valdez spill.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 52   ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS VALDEZ OIL SPILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it disturbs me to have to stand in the House today and speak on this issue, because it is a sorrowful
day for this House and Parliament to have to debate this issue. As one of my colleagues pointed out earlier tonight, it has come to this-after 22 years of warnings of environmental catastrophe, predictions by environmentalists and previous provincial administrations of looming environmental damage to the West Coast of British Columbia, of requests that supertanker traffic not be allowed to move throughout the waters close to the inter-tidal zones of the B.C. coast, the inevitable has finally happened.
There is a tendency for the Members in this House toward hyperbole. Sometimes the Members tend to embellish their arguments. In the discussion here tonight that has not been the case.
The issue tonight is truly a disaster of international and global proportions. With the accident at Valdez, we have let loose an ecological and environmental time bomb that we cannot control. We might have controlled it had there been immediate action taken by both the U.S. Government and the Canadian Government before the high-end distillates left the oil mass to create a sticky, globular mass half the size of Nova Scotia, 2,700 square kilometres of sticky, gooey, oily mess adrift on the high seas. No one can predict, certainly not the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) because he cannot even predict when planes will come in on time at the Toronto airport, what will happen to that mass as it drifts on the high seas in the winds and the tides.
The argument with respect to the direction that the oil mass will follow is simply conjecture.
I say to the Minister of the Environment that there is no way he or anyone in the Government can guarantee the people of British Columbia and the people of Canada that the drifting mass of oil will not impact on the B.C. coast at some point in the future. They cannot predict what will happen, and because of that the environmental integrity of the B.C. West Coast is in jeopardy at this very moment.
I want to talk for a moment about the Queen Charlottes, islands that are well known to people in British Columbia and people throughout the globe. It is a surrealistic place that is separated from the B.C. mainland by 100 kilometres of open water. It has been a refuge from the full impact of the last Ice Age. The islands house a unique ecological system, self-contained flora and fauna. It contains the world's largest black bear, the world's second highest eagle nest density, otter, wandering shrew, sea lion, seal, harbour porpoise, per-

April 4, 1989
egrine falcon, migrating whales, deer, elk, muskrat, raccoon, and the list goes on.
With spring and coho salmon fishing off the coast of Masset and Skidgate Islands, the Charlottes are truly an environmental heritage for British Columbia and for all of Canada, a way of life for the Haida nation. The area is a veritable treasure-house of environmental and tourist-related activities. To give you an example, people will pay over $2,000 for a boat trip around South Moresby Island. The people who visit these islands are the same people who go trekking in Nepal or on safaris in Africa. They are world-wide travellers, and they are flocking to the Queen Charlottes because of the pristine beauty and unspoiled wilderness that is offered there. These islands have won international recognition as an invaluable environmental and recreational resource. The United Nations has claimed a portion of the islands in the South Moresby area as a world heritage site. Our own federal Government has realized the value of the islands in its negotiations with the Province of British Columbia to make the South Moresby area a national park reserve.
I want to read a quote from National Geographic, 1987, that said:
The Queen Charlotte Islands cradled off British Columbia's West Coast are among the globe's rare jewels. A dagger-shaped assemblage of 150 islands, the Charlottes are a wilderness of the first rank abounding in treasures.
This jewel of British Columbia's north coast is threatened by a needless tragedy. That tragedy as a result of the oil spill at Valdez may well threaten the sensitive and fragile environmental and ecological systems that are on that island. When you look at the map, you find that the first land mass south of the Alaska Panhandle that the oil could possibly impact is the Queen Charlotte Islands.
Fifty million litres-half the size of Nova Scotia- I say to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard), the devastation that has been created, if it impacts on those islands, could be felt for years or decades. If this spill is allowed to foul the shorelines of the Charlottes, we will not only witness the widespread devastation to marine life but also the devastation to the economic and recreational resources of those islands. Who is going to want to fish on an island that is awash in oil? Who is going to want to visit it?
The impact of a major spill on these islands could wipe out a growing tourism trade that is only starting to be
realized and felt in its true potential. To give you an example, a recent travel survey in British Columbia has shown that the most frequent, single, main purpose of trips in northern B.C. is touring. In the northwest section of the province, which includes the Charlottes, touring was preferred by 70 per cent of the respondents. The cruise ship trade now nets British Columbia about $70 million a year with coastal runs up to Alaska. It carries about 15 per cent of the 2.3 million passengers that are cruising annually world-wide.
We have a major resource in our tourism right throughout the coast. The entire tourism industry is threatened by this drifting mass of oil. I say to the Minister that this Government must act now. It must act immediately to avert further environmental catastrophe. We cannot afford to make the same mistake that was made on the West Coast. This Government's inaction toward this looming disaster has been embarrassingly inadequate. The Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) and this Government must get off their duffs and develop an appropriate response to this and future environmental emergencies, because there will be future environmental emergencies.
We demand a full public inquiry into the West Coast oil spills and an inquiry into the inadequacies of this Government's response to those emergencies; the development of effective emergency response mechanisms for the containment of such toxic spills and the consideration of a moratorium on supertanker traffic in the immediate vicinity of Canada's inter-tidal waters; and lastly, a renewed commitment to the development of alternative emergency sources that will lessen the environmental impact on the use of fossil fuels. The people of British Columbia and the people of Canada deserve no less than this action from this Government.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 52   ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS VALDEZ OIL SPILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have sat here now this evening for the last five and a half hours or thereabouts and I have been struck with sympathy for my colleagues and their concern over this tragic incident on the West Coast of Canada. I need not remind this House that Canada is a three-ocean country and, indeed, I am sure our dimensions will extend in those directions.
April 4, 1989

This tragic oil spill on the West Coast that has sparked this debate hardly needs review here this evening. It has been mentioned many times. Reviewing it from the perspective of a sailor, we are talking about the grounding of a vessel in good visibility, in reasonably good weather. We are talking about a large vessel. You would appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that it is three times the length of a football field. When the captain decides he wants to stop it takes between two and three ship lengths depending on what speed that ship is going at. It is very difficult to manouvre. In fact, it manouvres in a turtle-like manner when everything is working well. But when the red flags start to go up things look worse and worse and worse.
We are looking at a situation in pilotage waters where ships are traditionally in danger and where every single precaution has been taken. Those precautions do not seem to have been taken in this particular instance.
These kinds of accidents are not confined to pilotage errors. They are not necessarily confined to errors in pilotage waters, that is, entering or leaving a confined harbour. There are other sorts of accidents, some that unfortunately put the Valdez oil spill well down, as was suggested earlier, in the world list in size. These accidents are not confined to the Pacific. Let me just relate a few.
Not too long ago four million barrels of oil from two oil wells spilled in the Gulf of Mexico and in the Persian Gulf. About 10 years ago two million barrels spilled as a result of a collision at sea between two supertankers near Trinidad and Tobago. I regret to remind you, Mr. Speaker, and this House that the record of the day was the Torrey Canyon which a few years ago sank off the coast of England and which spilled almost one million barrels of oil. I further regret that it was reported that the various emulsions used and sprayed on the water to contain this oil spill did more damage to the sea life and marine life than the oil spill itself.
In the case of the Exxon Valdez it involved, as we have been told this evening, 240,000 barrels. It has a potential effect on 800 fishermen in season and about 400 tourists, to say nothing of the tragic and decimating effect it has on the marine life and the sea life, and all the other kind of life in that area.
I have would just like to pose a question here this evening to all of us. What happens if there is an oil spill disaster resulting from our Hibernia project off the coast of Newfoundland when it comes into effect? We are looking at an entirely different dimension. We are looking at a lot more than 240,000 barrels of oil. We are
looking at a lot more people and a lot more marine life. We are looking at 25,000 fishermen and 6,000 people involved in tourism. We are looking at $350 million in tourism alone. We are looking at the possible disastrous effect on the northern cod which terminates roughly on the Nose of the Bank, the possible decimation of the salmon species, the capelin species, and many other species of fish which abound off the coast of Newfoundland.
Let me not forget the Arctic. My hon. friend from Nunatsiaq referred to a spill in the Arctic, the Northwest Passage. There was a spill recently at the other end of the globe down in the Antarctic. I need not remind anyone here this evening of the disastrous effect that might have as well.
I had the unfortunate personal experience as a young commander to be involved in the clean-up of the Arrow disaster which took place in Chedabucto Bay in Nova Scotia in the spring of 1970. It was not a pleasant experience. It was not a rewarding task. It was impromptu and it was ad hoc. I remember saying to myself at the time: "Please, God, if this ever happens again let us be prepared".
I am concerned that the oil spill severity off Vancouver Island was underestimated. I am referring now to the January spill. It was underestimated to the point that it took government workers from three to five days to become seriously involved. In the meantime, exasperated citizens, most of them volunteers, had already begun the clean-up work. In the case of the Exxon Valdez clean-up efforts I believe the Governor of Alaska referred to the clean-up methods as slow and inadequate.
Why do these efforts to contain disasters of this nature always have to be disorganized and impromptu? We should be ready. We know it is not a question of if; it is a question of when. In 1973 the statisticians said the probability of a big Alaska oil spill was 50 per cent in 20 years. It turned out to be 100 per cent in 16 years.
I submit there is an urgent need to bring all our national resources to bear. There is a need for contingencies. We need more research and development in this area. We need better international arrangements. We need a military-civilian contingency plan to cope with these things. We need better national regulations and stiffer penalties for those who ignore them. We are going to need money. I see no reason why we cannot demand that the oil companies which are making the profits put up the money right now.

April 4, 1989
In conclusion, this giant tragic oil spill now washing ashore possibly on the shores of Canada, on the West Coast of Canada, reveals the vulnerability of our three oceans to the risk of tanker transport of oil. We live in a three-ocean country. We need a three-ocean perspective which will include a three-ocean oil spill contingency plan now.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 52   ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS VALDEZ OIL SPILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased at the opportunity of speaking to this House again, and I am just unhappy about the fact that we do have to speak about such a disaster as we have been witnessing. I think about the geography of my riding, which is bounded on the north by the Fraser River, on the west by the Straits of Georgia, and on the south by Boundary Bay, and across Boundary Bay we have the Cherry Point refinery which was referred to by the Member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) and this is of course one of the termini of the Alaska oil that we have been discussing tonight. All the west side of my riding is very delicate from a natural point of view and we have the whole Fraser estuary there that is very sensitive to any spills or whatever may happen to it.
During the years I have had the privilege of working out on the West Coast in many different areas. I have worked from Carmenolite in the south up the Markley Sound where the recent oil spill was. I worked up into Niska Sound and into the Patsino area. So I am very familiar with what the terrain is like, and I can really understand what happened with the oil spill on the West Coast in January. I have also had the privilege of working in Fort Simpson which is the last Indian reserve before the Alaska Panhandle and the village of Metlakatla. I have seen the isolation, I have seen the desolation and I have seen the beauty of the West Coast of Canada and would submit, Mr. Speaker, that we have a real disaster at this time in the Alaska Panhandle and in southeastern Alaska. It is an ecological disaster. It is of a magnitude which I think most of us cannot understand. We have never envisioned it. We have not seen it and so I think that we can only go by pictures and our knowledge of the geography of that area. But I think we need to recognize, Mr. Speaker, that this was in American waters.
It was an American ship. It was handled by American people and I do not understand how the Opposition today have been trying to make political gain from such a
natural ecological disaster. They have been asking for a Minister's resignation. The Minister had nothing to do with it. It was a different country. It was an area over which he had no control whatsoever. They have complained about the lack of government action, and yet I believe that the Government has done everything that it possibly could do in both of these disasters on the West Coast.
I think we need to ask the question, what could the Government have done that it did not do? First of all, we have been criticized because we did not rush in with extra equipment, with manpower, with ships, and then we have to recognize that indeed these were American waters and we must recognize American sovereignty. When we offered help and it was accepted, then we moved in to do what we could do. It was mentioned that we could have supplied them with booms. Yet we recognized that once that oil had escaped from around the ship and was out into the open ocean and the winds picked up to 100 kilometres an hour, the oil booms were completely useless in that type of situation.
We have been talking about chemicals and we have just mentioned, or the Opposition has just mentioned, that the chemicals did more damage than they do good in many situations. They have been criticized because we did not use mechanical skimmers and again these were not asked for, and we recognized that with the mehanical skimmers that they did have, that they were only able to salvage approximately 3,500 barrels of oil out of the complete spill. I think what we need to recognize is the tremendous magnitude of the spill that did occur and the necessity, as soon as something like that does happen, of attacking the spill with energy, and because this did not happen in Canadian waters and because it was well away from population centres, this was unable to be done as well as this Government would have liked to have had it done.
I think we need to recognize the geography of the country and. the sparseness of the population. The ruggedness of the coastline makes it just impossible to clean the beaches, to cleanse the birds, to clean up the messes that were there, and again we recognize the part that the weather had to play in this disaster with winds that blew the oil around, that prevented the skimmers and everything from working. It is something that has to be experienced to realize the strength of the winds and the tides in that particular area.
April 4, 1989

I think what all this points out to us, Mr. Speaker, is that the most important thing in an oil spill is prevention, and I think that if anything good does come out of this debate tonight, it is the fact that we may be able to develop some better methods of prevention. I think the reason is obvious why we need to do this. With the size of the tankers that are economically essential in this day and age, an immediate response is necessary.
Perhaps we should be considering making double hulls mandatory on all tankers that are plying our waters. Perhaps we should be discussing having mandatory blood tests for all those in command of ships, and we could well imagine the shouts of disaster and infringement of civil rights that we would be hearing if this indeed were passed into law, and we know very well where the loudest protests would be coming from.
Perhaps we need to examine the traffic patterns of shipping off our coasts. As I mentioned, my riding is particularly sensitive, and perhaps we do need to re-examine and make sure that those traffic patterns that we have for our shipping lines are the best ones that are available. Perhaps the time has come to re-examine the use of pipelines in place of ships, the tankers that we are using at the present time, and as I mentioned, perhaps again we need to consider changing our regulations for ships that are using Canadian waters.
I agree that we must make those corporations that are responsible for these types of spills and disasters accountable for the damage which they have done. I think also that we need to conduct more research. We need to make our navigation safer. We recognize again that the ship had the best navigation aids available, but because of true and human error we still had the accident that occurred. We must continue to do research and clean up. We must continue to do research in our shipbuilding. Can we build these tankers to be more safe so if they are punctured in some way that they will not create the pollution that this one has created at the present time?
In summary, Mr. Speaker, let me just say that indeed we have a disaster. I think that again it will be a long time before we can fully comprehend the magnitude of that disaster, and I think that one of the best things that we can salvage from this thing is knowledge that we can use to prevent it from happening again.
I have extreme confidence, one hundred per cent confidence in our Ministers and in our Government. I can see no reason whatsoever to call upon the Minister of the Environment to resign. He did everything that he possible could in this situation. I can see no reason why our Transport Minister should in any way be under a cloud. He did everything that he possibly could, and I think that our Fisheries and Oceans Minister again was fully aware at all times of what was happening during this whole disaster and that the whole government ministerial staff operated without fault. I cannot think of any areas where they should have moved and they did not, and where they should not have moved where they did, and I think again that the Throne Speech that we have heard just yesterday emphasizes this Government's role in improving and helping our environment. I think that the world will unfold in its proper order and I believe that, because of this, Canada will be a better and safer place. Thank you.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hour is late, but I believe that the emergency debate which we have been involved in this evening is one of the most important debates to come before Parliament in the 10 years I have had the honour of representing the community of Burnaby.
On Friday, in Vancouver, my colleagues and I from the New Democratic Party announced at a press conference that we would be calling for an emergency debate as soon as the House was back in session the following Monday, which was yesterday, and that this would be a top priority for us as New Democrats.
I want to pay tribute to the work done by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), our spokesperson on the environment for the New Democratic Party, in successfully persuading the Speaker of the vital importance of this question not just to British Columbians but to all Canadians.
In calling for an emergency debate we are focusing on two fundamental questions, questions which are inextricably linked. One was the response of the Government of Canada to the oil spill off the west coast of Vancouver Island, which occurred on December 22. That was a spill of some 175,000 litres.

April 4, 1989
Of course, the primary focus of our concern at this time is the disasters off the coast of Alaska in Prince William Sound on March 24, the disaster of the Exxon Valdez with a spill of over 50 million litres of oil.
I say that these two spills are linked because the reality is that we are dealing with a system in which global oil companies have only one objective, that is, the maximization of their global profits. In attempting to maximize their global profits they have, time after time, displayed utter contempt for the environment of this fragile planet.
When we talk about the importance of bringing to justice those who were responsible, both in the criminal courts and in the civil court, I say that the ultimate responsibility for this corporate negligence, for this corporate murder, lies squarely in the boardrooms of Exxon, with the corporate directors who have shown such utter contempt for our environment in their desire to maximize their corporate profits. They must be brought to justice. They must be charged criminally if there is to be any justice at all in dealing with this terrible ecological disaster.
In early January I visited the west coast of Vancouver Island. I visited with a number of my colleagues, including the Speaker of the House himself. I want to thank the Speaker for having organized the particular visit. While I was there I spoke with volunteers who were working against incredible odds. They were volunteers from my constituency of Burnaby-Kingsway, as well as volunteers from literally right across Canada. I met with workers from the Coast Guard, and I want to commend both the volunteers and the workers from the Coast Guard who put in hour after hour of dedication and energy.
However, I also want to ask the questions in the House that they were asking. The volunteers were asking on that beach, as they were struggling to deal with the devastation of the environment, why they struggled alone. Where were the Canadian Armed Forces? Why were they not called in by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) or by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) to assist in this clean-up at the earliest possible opportunity? The volunteers who were there were asking these questions.
I believe the only sensible response to that and many other questions that arise from the west coast oil spill is to heed the call not just by New Democrats, but by environmentalists, native people and many other Canadians, for a full public inquiry into all aspects of this terrible tragedy. Native people on the west coast of Vancouver Island, native people on Haida Gwaii on the Queen Charlottes and elsewhere have warned us for years of the dangers of an oil spill of this nature.
Indeed, I remember a beautiful sunny day in late January standing on a beach on the northern coast of Haida Gwaii of the Queen Charlottes and looking across Dixon Entrance with a number of friends from the Haida nation. We spoke of the disaster off the west coast of Vancouver Island. They asked me to imagine the terrible tragedy if there were ever to be a similar oil spill from the Alaskan tankers which daily ply the coast. That imagined scenario is now a reality. That is what we New Democrats are pleading with the Government to recognize as well.
I was shocked when I heard the speech of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon), saying that there is no conceivable way that this spill can reach Canadian waters. I was shocked when I heard the Minister of Transport today saying that it is 1,000 kilometres away so we need not worry about it. I looked at a map of that area, and I know that the Minister of the Environment has looked at the same map. I would hope that they would recognize that if there is any change whatsoever in the winds or the currents this could pose a serious threat to the environment of Canada and the rivers that flow very close to that area. All of them are threatened.
If there is to be any possible risk that this spill will in fact move into Canadian waters, this spill which many of my colleagues have reminded the House is half the size of Nova Scotia, we are simply suggesting that the Government take steps to be ready.
We failed miserably to take those basic steps in dealing with the oil spill off the west coast of Vancouver Island. We stood by, believing that it would not come and would wash out to the ocean. It was too late when finally the oil started to wash up on the shores of the west coast. I have hiked the west coast trail. I have kayaked in Nootka Sound. I have camped at Long Beach. To see firsthand the results of that devastation was very painful for all of us. We do not want to see that again.
I plead with the Minister of the Environment to take the steps that are necessary. Have the containment booms in place. Have the contingency plans available for
April 4, 1989

clean up. Do the testing now of waters in that area to ensure that we know the base levels so that we are ready in the event that disaster strikes.
As well, we should surely recognize that the call by some for drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife refuge must be stopped. If ever we have a lesson to be learned it is not to allow that drilling to take place. I was very saddened to hear President Bush insisting that it was going to go ahead. Again, that mindless drive for profit at all cost must be resisted.
I listened to the eloquence of the Elon. Member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Anawak), the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Ms. Blondin), and my colleague, the Hon. Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin). I have spoken with Norma Kassi, the MLA for the area who has been so clear and forceful in expressing concern on behalf of native people in that community. I have talked with those who have asked why there are at least no double bottomed tankers to ensure that the transportation is a little safer.
In closing, I want to reiterate our call for a full public inquiry into both the west coast oil spill and the events surrounding the Government's lack of effective response to the Alaskan oil spill.
I recently met with a group of children, grade three students, at Stoney Creek Elementary School in my constituency, and student after student asked me why did it happen, how did it happen. I say that our Government owes the people of Canada an explanation, and I want to plead again with the Government to allow that inquiry to take place. Let us ensure that those children who ask those questions and their children inherit a planet, a country, a province, which respects the environment and does not destroy it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for the opportunity to participate in this most important debate, this emergency resolution on the Alaskan oil spill. To me, the discussion tonight points out clearly the contrast between how Members on this side of the House would deal with an issue like this and how Members opposite would suggest they would handle the issue.
We have on the one hand the attitude of Members opposite and the pious and patronizing attitudes of the Ministers and their comments. On this side of the House, I am proud that it is the New Democrats who have raised this issue, and particularly the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) who has spoken so eloquently on this issue and who I think has the admiration of all Hon. Members for speaking so clearly and for explaining to all of us how important this issue is. We appreciate his attendance here tonight.
I think the Minister should have provided leadership on this issue and should not be running to try to catch up. In fact, government Members have been running in the last two days since this session began. Yesterday, they fumbled with the Throne Speech, and tonight, they have fallen on their face in their participation in this debate.
I want to respond just briefly to some of the comments raised by the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) about the Government led by the now Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca (Mr. Barrett), a Government that introduced milestones in environmental protection. I am talking about the environment and land use committee and about the agricultural land reserve, policies that took a leadership role in that time, in that province and in this country today.
There was talk from Hon. Members opposite about how wonderful this Throne Speech was in its comments about the environment. I cannot let this opportunity go by without saying that there was not a single mention in it of our greatest environmental heritage, our forests. I challenge Hon. Members opposite to read that Throne Speech and to see if forestry is mentioned once. There is not a single mention of it.
Despite promises after promises, and after two elections now, for a commitment to legislate a full Department of Forests, there was no mention in this Throne Speech about that most important goal for British Columbia and the Government. Six forestry agreements expired across Canada on April Fool's Day, and that makes some sense for the Government across the way. There is nothing for forestry and there is nothing for the environment.
I remember the debate 22 years ago about the oil tanker traffic and oil moving down the coast in the tankers and the threat to the environment and the comments made by people to those who were concerned

April 4, 1989
about the environment. Of course, it is trendy now to talk about the environment, but there were people then and there are people now, perhaps on both sides of the Elouse, who are concerned about this issue.
We raised those issues then because we suggested and the evidence pointed out that a spill such as that which has happened in Valdez would happen either there or off Vancouver Island or in the Strait of Juan de Fuca, and it has happened. We are dealing with a tanker that was supposed to be of the latest technology. There were people on the bridge who, as far as we know and from all of the news reports, were not supposed to be there. Oil companies have given commitments that they have not lived up to. This has pointed out to Canadians and certainly to Members of the House that this Government, in its failure to respond adequately to the oil spill off the west coast of Vancouver Island, and certainly in speeches and comments from Ministers tonight, is not prepared now to deal with a massive oil spill if it should happen off the west coast of British Columbia again or in the future.
Our debate tonight is to point out the need for the Government to plan. We have not blamed the Government for the oil spill as some Hon. Members and in fact some Ministers have suggested. What we are calling for is an inquiry to look into the issues that have been raised tonight, and the very fact that the Minister has failed to respond to the letter of Januaiy 31 from my colleague, the Hon. Member for Saanich-Gulf Islands (Ms. Hunter), about an inquiry, gives us an indication of the concern that this Government has over the threat to our coast from oil spills. Our call is a responsible one and one that can benefit all sides of the House, the Government and the Opposition and particularly the people of the Province of British Columbia and the people of Canada.
I want to sum up with the comments of the Hon. Member for Burnaby-Kingsway (Mr. Robinson) about the Hon. Members from B.C. who who have raised this issue and made it an issue in the House. We appreciate the support from Hon. Members across Canada who have spoken on this debate tonight. We look forward to that debate continuing and to their ongoing support as we continue to press this Government, and we trust that it will hear our pleas and will act urgently on this matter.

speechtext:
The situation in the Gulf of Alaska is one that has been portrayed tonight by both sides of the House as a real disaster. It is that. I do not think a single Hon. Member has risen who has not concurred with that.
Even though my riding does not bound on any of the ocean waters-Cariboo-Chilcotin is large but it does not reach the coast-people there are also concerned, though not the environmentalists, not people you would expect to be hearing from. The last call I received was from a secretary in one of the mills. She explained to me that she did not know what I could do about it, but she hoped that there was something that I would be able to contribute. She expressed frustration, she expressed concern and I think it is probably typical of so many of the people who live not only in the Cariboo but of course all over British Columbia and right across Canada.
Why do they see this as such a disaster? Anybody who has sailed the coast of British Columbia, has dug for clams or shucked oysters in one of the Salt Spring Islands, or has had the fortune I had of working years ago when I was a youth and stopping in at all the ports along the west coast of Vancouver Island, would recognize that it is not just the Gulf of Alaska that they are thinking of. It is the proximity of that spill to the previous one off the coast of Washington which of course did impact on some of the British Columbia coast. It is a spectre. Any thinking British Columbian recognizes that with those oil ships plying our coast, that spill could have been in our own waters. We all recognize that that would have been a disaster that none of us would want to face.
We have recognized tonight from all those who have spoken that none of the three parties have a comer on concern about this environmental disaster. I do not think anyone should try to make a political comer out of this. I think the sensible speakers from all Parties have tended to agree that this is a common concern, that we should be looking at this in a positive manner, and that we should be taking from it what we can and coming out stronger.
The emergency debate tonight recognized by the Speaker as being necessary is, in my opinion, probably one of the best things that could have happened now. I was surprised to see that a matter of this much urgency to Canadians was recognized by this House and spoken to as it has been for most of the evening with three to five Ministers in attendance right through. I am impressed with that.
I think the immediate situation with the Alaska spill has been addressed by many Members from both sides of the House. We recognize that there are only certain
April 4, 1989

actions that can be taken. The responsibility for the accident was outside Canadian hands. We recognize now that if there is any potential for harm to Canadian waters or Canadian land we have to be prepared to act. We have heard our Ministers address that. They have gone further than that. That is really what concerns us here tonight. It is not the immediate spill but the spectre of what could have been. We want to know that we are prepared.
We have heard our Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) indicate that he is prepared and will conduct a full review of all of our procedures and regulations to ensure they are adequate to a potential situation that we all fear. I do not want to repeat what everyone else has said, but the Government has placed the environment as its top priority in the Throne Speech and some of the programs that were implemented in the previous session have been mentioned.
We did adopt the Canadian Environmental Protection Act which is considered to be a leader in environment protection in the world. Within three years, we will virtually eliminate all leaded gasoline, and in five years the industrial sulphur dioxide will be cut by 50 per cent. By the end of the century we have set the complete elimination of chemicals that affect our ozone layer. We have doubled the federal contribution for cleaning up
the Great Lakes and of course, as has been seen by so many reporting in the press, we have become one of the world leaders, if not the world leader, in pushing for environmental reform.
I think this debate tonight emphasizes the priority the Government has placed on the environment. I am proud to say that I am part of the Government that has been taking the action it has and will continue to take the action that will be required by all Canadians.
I would like to close on a positive note that if we took the essence of most of the speeches tonight and consolidated them-I suggest the Ministers might get their staff to do that-the essence of the discussions will form a very valuable contribution to the environmental program that our Minister is contemplating.
